comment: The section treats individual agency mainly as direct personal action. In practice, some people exercise agency with support or through an authorised representative, including during temporary illness, disability, cognitive decline or other changes in functional ability. Without a standard delegation model, countries and applications will recreate proxy access inconsistently, increasing privacy, safety and exclusion risks.

public.text: The section treats individual agency mainly as direct personal action. In practice, some people exercise agency with support or through an authorised representative, including during temporary illness, disability, cognitive decline or other changes in functional ability. Without a standard delegation model, countries and applications will recreate proxy access inconsistently, increasing privacy, safety and exclusion risks.
public.suggestedRevision: Add after line 370: “While the legal rules governing representation remain matters for national law and policy, the architecture should be capable of representing and enforcing supported and delegated access where permitted by law. It should distinguish assistance provided under the individual’s direction from authority exercised by an authorised representative, and support granular, purpose-limited, time-bound where appropriate, revocable and auditable permissions, including verification of the representative and the source of authority. Countries should also assess whether existing legal and regulatory frameworks adequately support these arrangements and undertake necessary reforms where gaps are identified.”
